questions.question: What are the factors favouring the formation of ionic bond?
questions.solution_html:
• Low ionization energy: The metal atom should have a low ionization energy, meaning
  • it requires little energy to lose its outermost electron(s) and form a positive ion (cation).
  • High electron gain enthalpy: The non-metal atom should have a high electron gain
  • enthalpy (or a high electron affinity), which is the energy change when an electron is
  • added to form a negative ion (anion). This means the non-metal readily accepts an
  • electron.
  • High lattice energy: The resulting ionic compound should have a high lattice energy.
  • Lattice energy is the energy released when a crystal lattice is formed from gaseous ions
  • and a high value indicates a very stable compound with strong ionic bonds.
questions.final_answer: and a high value indicates a very stable compound with strong ionic bonds

questions.question: Write notes on simple distillation (b) fractional distillation.
questions.solution_html:
• Simple distillation and fractional distillation are both separation techniques that work
  • by exploiting differences in the boiling points of liquids in a mixture. The key difference
  • is that fractional distillation is used for liquids with similar boiling points, while simple
  • distillation is for liquids with widely different boiling points.
  • Simple Distillation
  • Simple distillation involves a single cycle of vaporization and condensation. It is
  • effective for
  • Separating a liquid from a non-volatile solute (e.g., obtaining pure water from salt
  • water).
  • Separating two miscible liquids if their boiling points differ by at least 25°C to 70°C
  • (or more, depending on purity requirements).
  • Fractional Distillation
  • Fractional distillation is a more advanced and efficient method used to separate
  • components with similar or close boiling points (a difference of less than 25°C). It uses
  • a special piece of equipment called a fractionating column, which is packed with
  • materials like glass beads or rings to increase the surface area.
  • This column allows for multiple, repeated cycles of vaporization and condensation
  • (known as theoretical plates) as the vapor rises.
  • Components with lower boiling points rise higher in the column before condensing and
  • being collected, while those with higher boiling points condense lower down and flow
  • back into the flask.

questions.question: Describe with examples primary standard and secondary standard.
questions.solution_html:
• Primary standards are highly pure, stable, and non-hygroscopic substances used to
  • calibrate secondary standards, while secondary standards are less pure, more reactive
  • and are standardized against a primary standard for routine analytical use. Primary
  • standards, like pure sodium carbonate, are used to determine unknown concentrations
  • accurately, whereas secondary standards, such as a standardized sodium hydroxide
  • solution, are used for everyday analyses like instrument calibration.
  • Primary standards Definition: Extremely pure substances with known properties used
  • to make a standard solution. Properties: High purity (often (99.9%). Highly stable and
  • not easily affected by air or moisture. Anhydrous (no water molecules attached). High
  • molecular weight, making them easier to weigh accurately. Low reactivity or not
  • reactive at all.
  • Examples: Sodium carbonate, potassium hydrogen phthalate, and pure metals.
  • Definition: Less pure substances or solutions that are standardized against a primary
  • standard. Properties: Less pure than primary standards. Less stable and potentially
  • reactive. Can be hygroscopic (absorb moisture from the air). Examples: Commercially
  • available sodium hydroxide (NaOH) and hydrochloric acid (HCl) solutions.
questions.final_answer: available sodium hydroxide (NaOH) and hydrochloric acid (HCl) solutions

questions.question: Write notes on Hydrogen bond (b) Van der Waal's forces.
questions.solution_html:
• (a) H-bonding, or hydrogen bonding, is a weak but important intermolecular force that
  • occurs when a hydrogen atom covalently bonded to a highly electronegative atom (like
  • oxygen, nitrogen, or fluorine) is attracted to another nearby electronegative atom.
  • Types of hydrogen bonds
  • Intermolecular hydrogen bonding: The hydrogen bond forms between two different
  • molecules. A classic example is the hydrogen bonding between separate water (H2O)
  • molecules.
  • Intramolecular hydrogen bonding: The hydrogen bond forms between two atoms within
  • the same molecule.
  • (b) Van der Waals forces are weak intermolecular forces that arise from temporary or
  • permanent fluctuations in electron distribution within molecules, causing transient or
  • permanent partial charges. These forces are weaker than covalent or ionic bonds and
  • can be separated into two main types: London dispersion forces, which occur in all
  • molecules due to random electron movement, and dipole-dipole interactions, which
  • occur between polar molecules with permanent charges.

questions.question: Write an essay on Ionisation enthalpy.
questions.solution_html:
• Ionization enthalpy is the minimum energy required to remove the outermost electron
  • from a gaseous atom, forming a positive ion. This energy is a measure of how tightly
  • an electron is held to the nucleus. Factors like the attraction between the nucleus and
  • electrons, electron repulsion, and effective nuclear charge all influence it. It decreases
  • down a group and increases across a period in the periodic table.
  • • Periodic trends
  • o Across a period: It generally increases from left to right because the increasing
  • nuclear charge pulls the electrons more tightly.
  • o Down a group: It decreases from top to bottom as the atomic radius increases
  • meaning the outermost electrons are farther from the nucleus and are shielded
  • by more inner electrons.
  • Factors that influence ionization enthalpy
  • • Nuclear charge: A higher nuclear charge increases the force of attraction on electrons
  • requiring more energy to remove them.
  • • Atomic radius: A larger atomic radius means the valence electrons are farther from the
  • nucleus, resulting in a weaker attraction and lower ionization enthalpy.
  • • Shielding effect: Inner-shell electrons "shield" the outer-shell electrons from the full
  • force of the nuclear charge. A greater shielding effect results in a lower ionization
  • enthalpy.
questions.source_exam: First Semester MGU-UGP/MGU-BBA/MGU-BCA Honours Examinations November 2025

questions.question: Give notes on Normality (b) Mole fraction (c) ppm and (d) ppb.
questions.solution_html:
• Normality
  • Definition: The number of equivalents of a solute per liter of solution.
  • Units: Equivalents/Liter (eq/L).
  • Use: Also called equivalent concentration, it is often used in acid-base and redox
  • titrations.
  • Mole fraction
  • Definition: The ratio of the number of moles of a component to the total number of
  • moles of all components in the solution.
  • Units: Unitless.
  • Parts per million (ppm)
  • Definition: A way to express very dilute concentrations, meaning one part of a
  • substance per one million parts of the total solution.
  • Units: Commonly expressed as milligrams per liter (mg/L) for solutions or milligrams
  • per kilogram (mg/kg).
  • Parts per billion (ppb)
  • Definition: A measure of concentration that signifies one part of a substance per one
  • billion parts of the total mixture.
  • Units: Commonly expressed as micrograms per liter (µg/L) for solutions or micrograms
  • per kilogram (µg/kg).
